name: CP2000
title: Proposed changes to your tax return
what: The income or payments reported to the IRS by employers, banks, brokers and others don't match what's on your return. The IRS is proposing changes, which usually means more tax, interest and possibly a penalty. It is not a bill and not a formal audit yet.
common: A missed 1099 (interest, dividends, freelance, stock sales)
Stock sales reported without cost basis
Retirement distributions or unemployment left off the return
todo: Compare every item on the notice to your records and your return
If you agree, sign the response form and pay or set up a payment plan
If you disagree in whole or part, send the response form with a signed explanation and documents
Don't file an amended return for these changes; respond to the notice instead
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice, usually 30 days. If you don't, the IRS sends a Statutory Notice of Deficiency and assesses the tax.

name: CP2501
title: Income on your return doesn't match IRS records
what: An earlier, informal version of the CP2000. The IRS found a difference between your return and information it received, and is asking you to explain before it proposes changes.
common: Unreported 1099 or W-2 income
Income reported on a different line or form than the IRS expected
todo: Check whether the income is already included somewhere on your return
Reply with an explanation and supporting documents, or agree that it was missed
Respond even if you think it's already correct, so it doesn't move to a CP2000
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice to avoid a CP2000.

name: CP14
title: You have a balance due
what: The first bill for unpaid tax. It shows the tax, penalties and interest owed as of the notice date. Interest and late-payment penalties keep growing until it's paid.
common: Return filed without full payment
Estimated payments missed or applied to the wrong year
A change the IRS made after processing your return
todo: Check that the balance is right, including any payments you made
Pay in full by the due date, or apply for a payment plan
If you disagree, contact the IRS at the number on the notice
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice (usually 21 days) to limit extra interest and penalties.

name: CP501
title: Reminder: you still have a balance due
what: A follow-up reminder that a balance is still unpaid after an earlier notice. Interest and penalties are still being added.
common: A CP14 that wasn't paid or answered
todo: Pay the balance or set up a payment plan
Contact the IRS if you've already paid or disagree
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. Next comes a CP503.

name: CP503
title: Second reminder: balance due
what: An urgent second reminder that a balance is unpaid. Ignoring it moves you closer to a notice of intent to levy.
common: Earlier balance-due notices not paid or answered
todo: Pay now or set up a payment plan
Call the number on the notice if you can't pay in full
Get help if you're facing several years of balances
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. Next comes a CP504.

name: CP504
title: Notice of intent to levy
what: The IRS intends to seize (levy) your state tax refund to pay the balance, and warns it may levy other property or rights. It can also lead to a federal tax lien.
common: Balance unpaid after CP14, CP501 and CP503
todo: Pay in full, or set up a payment plan right away
If you can't pay, ask about hardship status or other options
Get professional help before a final levy notice arrives
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. The next step is usually a final notice with appeal rights (LT11 or Letter 1058).

name: LT11 / Letter 1058
title: Final notice of intent to levy and your right to a hearing
what: The IRS's final notice before it can levy wages, bank accounts and other assets. It also gives you the right to a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals.
common: Unpaid balances after earlier notices
todo: Pay in full or arrange a payment plan
To protect your appeal rights, file Form 12153 (Request for a Collection Due Process hearing) on time
Talk to an Enrolled Agent or other tax professional now
deadline: You have 30 days from the notice date to request a CDP hearing. Missing it limits your options.

name: CP90
title: Final notice of intent to levy
what: A final notice that the IRS intends to levy your assets, such as wages, bank accounts, Social Security or other income, and your right to a Collection Due Process hearing.
common: Unpaid balances after earlier notices
todo: Pay or arrange a payment plan
File Form 12153 to request a hearing if you disagree or need time
Get professional help right away
deadline: 30 days from the notice date to request a Collection Due Process hearing.

name: CP3219A / Letter 3219
title: Statutory Notice of Deficiency
what: The IRS has determined you owe additional tax and is formally telling you of your right to challenge it in U.S. Tax Court. Often follows an unanswered CP2000 or audit.
common: No response to a CP2000
Audit changes you didn't agree to
todo: Decide whether you agree with the changes
If you disagree, file a petition with the U.S. Tax Court before the deadline
Don't ignore it: once the deadline passes the tax is assessed
deadline: 90 days from the notice date to petition Tax Court (150 days if addressed to you outside the U.S.). The deadline cannot be extended.

name: CP11
title: We changed your return: you owe money
what: The IRS found a math or calculation error on your return, corrected it, and you now owe tax.
common: Miscalculated credits (child tax credit, earned income credit)
Recovery or stimulus credit errors
Arithmetic errors
todo: Compare the IRS's changes to your return
If you agree, pay or set up a payment plan
If you disagree, contact the IRS within 60 days and they'll reverse the change, though they may then examine it further
deadline: 60 days from the notice date to dispute the change.

name: CP12
title: We changed your return: your refund changed
what: The IRS corrected one or more errors on your return. Your refund is now different, or you now get a refund instead of owing.
common: Miscalculated credits
Withholding or estimated payment amounts entered incorrectly
todo: Review the changes against your return
If you agree, no action is needed
If you disagree, contact the IRS within 60 days
deadline: 60 days from the notice date to dispute the change.

name: CP59
title: You didn't file a tax return
what: IRS records show you didn't file a return for the year shown, and you may need to. Not filing can lead to penalties and the IRS filing a substitute return for you.
common: A return was never filed
A return was filed under a different SSN or name
A return was sent but not processed
todo: File the missing return right away
If you already filed, send a copy and the date filed
If you weren't required to file, explain why using the response form
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice.

name: CP05
title: We're reviewing your return
what: The IRS is reviewing your return to verify income, withholding, credits or business income before issuing your refund. It does not mean you did something wrong.
common: Random or automated verification of withholding and credits
todo: No action is needed unless the IRS asks for more information
Keep your W-2s, 1099s and records handy
Wait for the follow-up notice
deadline: No response required. Review typically takes several weeks.

name: CP75
title: Audit: documents needed for credits
what: The IRS is auditing your return and holding part or all of your refund until you prove eligibility for credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit, or certain deductions.
common: Earned Income Tax Credit
Child tax credit or dependent claims
Business income on Schedule C
todo: Gather the documents listed (school or medical records showing children lived with you, business records)
Send them by the deadline using the enclosed form
Get help if you're unsure what proves eligibility
deadline: Respond by the date on the notice, usually 30 days.

name: Letter 5071C
title: Verify your identity
what: The IRS received a return with your name and SSN and needs you to confirm it was you who filed it, to protect against identity theft. Your return and refund are on hold until you verify.
common: Possible identity theft
Changes in your filing pattern
todo: Verify online at the IRS identity verification site listed in the letter, or by phone
Have the letter, your prior-year and current-year returns and supporting documents ready
If you didn't file the return, say so: it may be identity theft
deadline: Verify as soon as possible. Your refund won't be released until you do.

name: Letter 4883C
title: Verify your identity by phone
what: Like Letter 5071C, the IRS needs to confirm your identity before processing a return filed under your name, but asks you to call.
common: Possible identity theft
todo: Call the number in the letter (only that number)
Have the letter, the return in question and your prior-year return ready
deadline: Call as soon as possible; processing stops until you do.

name: Letter 12C
title: We need more information to process your return
what: Your return is missing information or forms, so the IRS can't finish processing it.
common: Missing Form 8962 for Marketplace health insurance (Form 1095-A)
Missing W-2 or withholding information
Missing schedules
todo: Send the requested form or information
Include a copy of the letter with your response
deadline: Respond by the date in the letter, usually 20 days, or your refund may be reduced.

name: Letter 566
title: Correspondence audit: first contact
what: The IRS is examining (auditing) specific items on your return by mail and is asking you to send documents to support them.
common: Deductions or credits that need proof
Business expenses
todo: Read which items are being examined
Send organized copies of receipts and records, never originals
Consider having an Enrolled Agent represent you
deadline: Respond by the date in the letter.

name: Letter 525
title: Proposed audit changes
what: After examining your return, the IRS is proposing changes, usually additional tax. You can agree, or disagree and provide more information or request an appeal.
common: Documents sent during an audit weren't enough
No response to an earlier audit letter
todo: Review the examination report
Sign the agreement form if you agree
If you disagree, send more information or request an Appeals conference
deadline: Usually 30 days from the letter date. After that, a Statutory Notice of Deficiency may follow.

name: CP49
title: Your refund was applied to a tax debt
what: The IRS used all or part of your refund to pay a balance you owe for another tax year.
common: Prior-year balance due
todo: Check which year the refund was applied to
If any refund remains, it will be sent separately
Contact the IRS if you think the debt was already paid
deadline: No response required unless you disagree.

name: CP71C
title: Annual reminder of a balance due
what: A yearly reminder that you still have an unpaid balance, which continues to grow with interest and penalties.
common: An older balance that's been in collection or put on hold
todo: Pay what you can or set up a payment plan
Ask about options if you can't pay
deadline: Act as soon as possible to stop interest and penalties growing.

name: CP521
title: Installment agreement payment reminder
what: A reminder of your monthly payment under an existing IRS payment plan, and your remaining balance.
common: Active installment agreement
todo: Make your payment by the due date
Consider setting up automatic payments
deadline: Pay by the due date shown.

name: CP523
title: Intent to end your payment plan and levy
what: The IRS intends to terminate your installment agreement, usually because payments were missed or new taxes went unpaid, and then levy your assets.
common: Missed monthly payments
A new balance due
Unfiled returns
todo: Bring payments current right away
File any missing returns
Call the IRS or get help to reinstate the agreement
deadline: Act by the date on the notice. You may have the right to appeal the termination.

name: CP161
title: Business balance due
what: Your business owes money for the tax period shown, often from a return processed with a balance, penalties or a math error.
common: Late filing or late payment penalties
Payroll tax deposits short or late
Math errors on the business return
todo: Check the balance against your payment records
Pay or set up a business payment plan
Request penalty relief if you qualify (for example, first-time abatement)
deadline: Pay by the date on the notice to avoid more interest and penalties.

name: CP2100 / CP2100A
title: Backup withholding: incorrect payee TINs
what: Sent to businesses that file 1099s. Some of the names and taxpayer ID numbers you reported don't match IRS records, and you may need to start backup withholding on those payees.
common: Contractors who gave a wrong SSN/EIN
Name changes or typos on 1099s
todo: Compare the list to your records
Send a B-notice to each listed payee with a new W-9
Start backup withholding (24%) if a payee doesn't respond in time
deadline: Send B-notices within 15 business days of receiving the notice.

name: CP575
title: Your new EIN (Employer Identification Number)
what: Confirmation that the IRS assigned an EIN to your business. Banks and others often ask for this letter. It isn't a problem notice.
common: Applying for an EIN online, by fax or by mail
todo: Keep it with your permanent business records
If you lose it, ask the IRS for Letter 147C to confirm your EIN
deadline: No response required.
